newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris says may help Belgium in Dassault probe.
newsitem.headline: Paris says may help Belgium in Dassault probe.

text.p: French Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou said on Wednesday that she was likely to hand over some secret documents requested by Belgium for a bribery probe against French warplane maker Serge Dassault.
The documents are the focus of a long-running dispute since France's former centre-right government refused to hand them over despite Belgian insistence.

"I believe that we will be able to send to Belgian justice part of these documents...probably a large part," Guigou of the new leftist government told Europe-1 radio a few hours before French President Jacques Chirac visits Belgium.
But she said the French government had still not determined whether or not national security was affected by all the documents requested by Belgium.
Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, due to meet Chirac after his arrival on Wednesday afternoon, earlier urged France to hand over the disputed documents.

"Both France and Belgium defend within the European Union the idea of a unified judicial area. The sending of the documents should take place in a more flexible way than it is happening now," Dehaene told France-Inter radio.

Belgian police are investigating allegations that Dassault Aviation paid 600 million Belgian francs ($17 million) to political parties to secure a contract to fit air defence systems to Belgian F-16 jets in the late 1980s.
Dehaene also said that Renault 's closure of a car plant in Belgium employing 3,100 people had been announced with "19th century" disregard for staff.

"The way this decision was taken and announced in the (Renault) company was totally unacceptable and more in line with labour relations of the 19th century than the 20th or the 21st centuries," Dehaene said.

But he struck a conciliatory note, saying of talks with former French Prime Minister Alain Juppe: "The position which he explained to me was the position that I would have defended if I was in his place. He told me that the company's autonomy was at stake, and that he must respect this."
The French state is the biggest shareholder in Renault with 46 percent.
